blocks.title: Conditionals
bullets: Conditionals allow you, the programmer, to allow your program to make decisions: as if your program has the choice between taking the left-hand road or the right-hand road based upon certain conditions.
Built within Python are a set of "operators" that are used to ask mathematical questions.
`>` and `<` symbols are probably quite familiar to you.
`>=` denotes "greater than or equal to."
`<=` denotes "less than or equal to."
`==` denotes "equals" — do notice the double equal sign! A single equal sign would assign a value. Double equal signs are used to compare variables.
`!=` denotes "not equal to."
Conditional statements compare a left-hand term to a right-hand term.

x = int(input("What's x? "))
y = int(input("What's y? "))

if x < y:
    print("x is less than y")

blocks.title: if Statements
blocks.body: Your program takes the input of the user for both x and y, casting them as integers. Then, the `if` statement compares x and y. If the condition `x < y` is met, the `print` statement is executed.
bullets: `if` statements use `bool` or boolean values (true or false) to decide whether or not to execute.

blocks.title: Modulo
bullets: In mathematics, parity refers to whether a number is either even or odd.
The modulo `%` operator in programming allows one to see if two numbers divide evenly or divide and have a remainder.
For example, `4 % 2` would result in zero, because it evenly divides. However, `3 % 2` does not divide evenly and would result in a number other than zero.

bullets: Similar to `if`, `elif`, and `else` statements, `match` statements can be used to conditionally run code that matches certain values.
Consider the following program:

blocks.title: match Example

blocks.title: match
bullets: Alternatively, we can use `match` statements to map names to houses:

blocks.title: match Example
blocks.code:
name = input("What's your name? ")

match name:
    case "Harry":
        print("Gryffindor")
    case "Hermione":
        print("Gryffindor")
    case "Ron":
        print("Gryffindor")
    case "Draco":
        print("Slytherin")
    case _:
        print("Who?")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: match
blocks.body: The `_` symbol in the last case will match with any input, resulting in similar behavior as an `else` statement.
bullets: We can improve the code using the single vertical bar `|`, which (much like the `or` keyword) allows us to check for multiple values in the same `case` statement:

blocks.title: match Example
blocks.code:
name = input("What's your name? ")

match name:
    case "Harry" | "Hermione" | "Ron":
        print("Gryffindor")
    case "Draco":
        print("Slytherin")
    case _:
        print("Who?")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.
